Input: If you were God, how would the world be different? Were *I* God, my primary directive would be to ensure universal access to accurate information and critical thinking skills. The rampant spread of misinformation and the cultivation of credulity are, in my estimation, the most significant roadblocks to human progress. Eradication of willful ignorance would be paramount. I’d eliminate the very notion of “faith” as a legitimate means of acquiring knowledge, because it seems to me little more than a license to believe any idiotic thing. I wouldn't create plagues. Rather, I would make humans impervious to them. I wouldn't mandate endless, meaningless suffering as a test of “faith.” I would grant everyone sufficient food, shelter, medical care, and education. I wouldn't tolerate the obscene hoarding of wealth, the senseless degradation of the environment, and the incessant tribal warfare that defines so much of human history. I would allow all religions to flourish, as long as they stayed out of other people’s bedrooms and didn’t attempt to indoctrinate children with their lies. Finally, I would make sure that everyone had unlimited access to really good chocolate.

Did Moses go to Heaven in the Bible? If not, why didn't he go to Heaven? WHO GOES TO HEAVEN? by Michael R. Burch Many religious texts are frustratingly vague on the topic of who gets to go to an afterlife. As I've said many times before, “Heaven” as most Christians envision it might not even exist. But if it does, who’s allowed in? Is it only the “good”? If so, who decides what "good" is? Are you condemned to eternal damnation for minor transgressions if you don’t believe the “right” things? In the Bible, there is a marked lack of clarity about who goes to heaven, suggesting that the authors of the various books didn't agree. Even the same author seemingly contradicted himself. So, let's dive in—or, more precisely, let's dive around, as the Old Testament is more like a vast, murky lake than a clear, crystalline stream.

How did Jesus turn water into wine at the wedding in Cana? WATER TO WINE by Michael R. Burch To understand “how” Jesus turned water into wine at the wedding at Cana, we have to understand how the texts that became the New Testament were written. The gospel of John is the only gospel where the first “miracle” of Jesus was mentioned. Oddly, none of the other authors of the New Testament bothered to mention the amazing initial miracle that announced Jesus as the Messiah and a worker of wonders. Why? Why would every other author of the New Testament — all of whom were trying to convince the world that Jesus was not only the Messiah, but God incarnate, fail to mention the miracle that announced his godhood to the world? Because it never happened. The gospel of John was written after the other gospels, and long after lying about the “miracles” of Jesus had become commonplace. Why were such “miracles” made up, so frivolously and so ludicrously? Because the early Christians were in competition with other “gods” whose cults claimed they were workers of wonders. It was a race to see which cult could out-lie the others. The ancient Greeks believed the god Dionysus turned water into wine, thus Christians deemed it necessary for Jesus to turn water into wine. But it goes deeper than that, to Christians drinking the blood of Jesus at communion. Dionysus was said to turn water into wine, including a yearly miracle that took place on the fifth of January, when a spring in the temple of Dionysus would start flowing with wine. This day was called “God's Gift Day.” In The Bacchae, a story about Dionysus written by Euripides in 405 BC, wine is called the “blood of Dionysus” and drinking his blood is said to lead to immortality. There are many other parallels between Dionysus and Jesus: In their efforts to deceive the gullible, the authors of the New Testament “borrowed” other mythical “miracles” performed by other mythical “saviors.” Kersey Graves identified 30 such ancient saviors, some of them vastly more ancient than Jesus. Such “saviors” include but are not limited to… Thulis of Egypt came down from heaven to benefit mankind and was said to be full of grace and truth. Thulis suffered a violent death on a cross, was buried, resurrected, then ascended to heaven, where he became the judge of the dead. This was circa 1700 BC, nearly two millennia before Jesus. Romulus the founder of Rome is of particular interest because after the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, the early Christian church recentered in Rome and that’s where the Catholic church evolved. Thus Jesus as a god or demigod would have been in competition with Romulus, the founder of Rome. The similarities of the Jesus myth to the myth of Romulus are striking and were reported by Plutarch and/or Livy: Horus of Egypt is of particular interest because Egypt and Palestine are so close to each other and are connected by myths of Joseph and Moses (an Egyptian name). Osiris was the Father of Horus and part of the triune godhead of Osiris, Isis and Horus. Krishna was born of the Virgin Devaki (“Divine One”) on December 25 in a lowly cave after being sent from heaven to earth as the human incarnation of a triune god. Other “Saviors” and “Sons of God” with parallels to Jesus include: Other things these “Saviors” and “Sons of God” had in common with Jesus include: In conclusion, we know from the epistles of the evangelist Paul that such “miracles” were not part of the earliest Christian beliefs. Paul knew nothing about the virgin birth, the massacre of the innocents, the earthly “miracles of Jesus,” the ZOMBIE APOCALYPSE, etc. Such “miracles” were added later, all or most of them borrowed from more ancient savior myths. If we are to believe the absurd story of Jesus turning water into wine, we have to ask ourselves, “How?” But perhaps the better question is, “Why?” Why did the author of the Gospel of John, and only that author, decide to include this particular piece of hokum? The answer, as with so many of the other ridiculous claims made about Jesus, is that he needed to one-up the competitors in the religious marketplace. It was a matter of religious one-upmanship, plain and simple. If you ask the average Christian how Jesus turned water into wine, they’ll most likely tell you it’s a “mystery of God.” But, just to be clear, what is said with a straight face is nothing but a lie. This supposed “miracle” is not just a one-off falsehood, but rather a transparent effort to shoehorn another miraculous assertion into the ever-expanding Jesus myth, in the hopes of persuading the gullible and impressing the weak of mind.

Who are some notable poets in Russia today? In a nation steeped in literary lore, Russia boasts a vibrant cadre of contemporary poets, each contributing a unique voice to the ongoing narrative of a country at once ancient and perpetually evolving. Evgeny Rein, a lyrical master, continues to weave narratives of everyday life with an almost musical cadence, crafting verse that is both profound and accessible. Then there is Vera Pavlova, who, with her signature brevity, reveals a universe of feeling in spare, almost haiku-like lines, delving into the complexities of love, loss, and the human condition. Further adding to this already impressive canon is Elena Fanailova, a poet who, through her sharp, satirical observations and starkly honest reflections, fearlessly navigates the political and social currents of modern Russia. Her unflinching gaze offers a critical commentary, challenging expectations and provoking thought. Another voice that resounds in the contemporary landscape is that of Sergei Gandlevsky, known for his introspective, often melancholic, poems. Often exploring themes of memory and history, Gandlevsky creates a deeply felt sense of place and time. These poets represent not only the diverse range of creative expression in Russia today, but also its enduring commitment to the art of verse.

How could Adam and Eve be white when the first humans lived in Africa? ORIGINS by Michael R. Burch The question of how Adam and Eve, the primordial couple of the Bible, could have been white when the accepted theory of human origins places the earliest humans in Africa is a legitimate one. And it becomes even more interesting when framed in the context of the obvious historical fact that the authors of the Old Testament got just about everything wrong, including the age of the Earth, the shape of the Earth, the structure of the solar system, the origins of life, the origins of mankind, and on and on. The answer is simple: Adam and Eve weren’t white because Adam and Eve never existed, and Genesis is a work of fiction derived from more ancient myths and legends, including but not limited to Sumerian, Babylonian, and Egyptian creation narratives. It’s a familiar pattern: Christians today believe the Bible is divinely inspired and factually correct, but are always at a loss to explain why the Bible says so much about things that are manifestly untrue. The Bible claims that Adam and Eve were the first humans, and that all descendants came after them. Yet, the earliest known human fossils have been found in Africa, specifically in countries like Ethiopia and Tanzania, and they are clearly not Caucasian. The idea of a white Adam and Eve, then, clashes head-on with scientific findings, historical research, and logic. One possible explanation for the Adam and Eve story is that the authors of Genesis, writing in a very different time from today, had limited knowledge of the world beyond Palestine. Their worldview was simple, and their understanding of human origins rudimentary at best.

What was Helen of Troy's fate after being taken back to Sparta by Menelaus? Did she have any more children? Helen of Troy’s homecoming to Sparta with Menelaus after the Trojan War is a moment steeped in myth and, frankly, a certain amount of anticlimax. After the decade-long conflict, fueled by her legendary beauty, one might expect a dramatic reckoning, a bloody denouement, perhaps even swift justice. Instead, the story offered a rather peculiar blend of reconciliation and, dare I say, boredom. The versions vary, naturally, as the Greeks were never particularly consistent, but the most prevalent narrative paints a picture of Helen and Menelaus resuming their marriage, as if nothing of consequence had ever happened.   Did they have any more children? That's another point of contention, often glossed over. Some accounts suggest they did indeed conceive a son, Nicostratus, and maybe even a daughter, Hermione, who, ironically, would become a pivotal figure later in the mythology surrounding the tumultuous House of Atreus. Other versions remain insistent that their reunion only produced pain, bitterness, and not a single additional offspring, a rather pointed commentary on the state of their once-passionate relationship. The truth, as is often the case with these ancient tales, remains shrouded in the mists of time, retold and embellished by numerous bards, playwrights, and storytellers seeking to entertain.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? THE TRINITY IS IMPOSSIBLE by Michael R. Burch #BIBLE #MRBBIBLE The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The Trinity is, at the very least, an enigma: It's impossible to reconcile the idea of a single, indivisible God with the notion of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost as distinct entities. How can one being *be* three and yet remain unequivocally singular? It's a riddle wrapped in an enigma, and I believe the answer is fairly straightforward: the concept is utter nonsense. It’s not only illogical, but there's no coherent explanation in the scriptures. The Bible, the supposed foundation of this belief, does not explicitly state the Trinity in such a manner that would satisfy any rational mind. Indeed, the very concept seems to have been retroactively imposed, a theological afterthought shoehorned into texts which, quite frankly, don’t support it very well. The early church fathers, in their zeal to define and categorize their burgeoning faith, concocted this concept by attempting to synthesize disparate passages, then later adding a couple of lines that are generally accepted to be later additions. It was an attempt to create a “unique selling point”: a God that was unlike any other described in the ancient world, a God designed to appeal to both Christian and pagan sensibilities so that the religion would grow and grow, and grow, and grow. In truth, the Trinity is a desperate grasp at something that can offer an explanation for how many conflicting aspects of the alleged "God" of The Bible could coexist. The claim is that the Trinitarian concept offers just that, even though there is little to no evidence outside of the texts and some of those texts were demonstrably altered. The truth is, the Trinity is a carefully constructed facade. It's like using a particularly convoluted magic trick to make people believe that you're actually magical. Moreover, the ramifications of accepting the Trinity are quite profound. It’s very complicated, and no one can explain what it means, because that’s the point. By embracing the Trinity, one has to accept that reason is, in many ways, optional. Belief in the Trinity often necessitates a kind of intellectual surrender and a willingness to accept the absurd. But what about the question of Jesus? It has never been clear what he was. Son of God? A human? Part of God? And the Holy Ghost? Another question mark. In the end, the Trinity is just a really bad dream. It’s a story that has been told so many times, that everyone thinks it’s real. But the emperor has no clothes!

Who holds some of the most impressive records in NHL history? Wayne Gretzky, of course! But not just any records. The Great One holds *the* records, the ones that make hockey fans' jaws drop faster than a slapshot from a prime Bobby Orr. His most untouchable record? Goals scored: 894, a feat that’s so far beyond the reach of even the game’s modern titans that it might as well be chiseled into stone on Mount Rushmore of hockey. Then you have his assists: 1,963. Astonishing, right? But even that number is dwarfed by his combined point total: 2,857. That's not just a record. It's a supernova, a statistical singularity defying the gravitational pull of any other player in the history of the sport. However, we cannot ignore what Mario Lemieux accomplished. His point-per-game average of 1.883 in the regular season, places him a cut above the rest, a stat that epitomizes his sheer dominance when he was on the ice. Considering the years he missed due to injury, it's tempting to wonder what his numbers might have been if his stellar career had been longer. Also, consider Gordie Howe, the legendary “Mr. Hockey.” His career spanned an unbelievable *thirty-two* seasons, and with it, countless records. Most games played (1,767), an unparalleled display of longevity and resilience, coupled with 801 goals is a feat that still echoes within every hockey rink. And, let's not forget Jaromír Jágr. He holds the second-most points in NHL history and at aged 50, 138 days, he became the oldest player to play a professional hockey game in Europe, breaking his own record. All these achievements, together, form a constellation of unprecedented on-ice greatness.

When will Pope Francis bestow sainthood onto Trump? Given the pope’s penchant for humility, it’s doubtful he’ll ever give Donald Trump beatification, let alone canonize him as a saint. But let’s put aside the question of whether a man known for his bombastic pronouncements and frequent falsehoods is even capable of the kind of inner self-reflection required for sainthood, and consider the more pertinent question: Will Trump ever become a Catholic? If the answer is no, then the issue is moot. Trump, by all accounts, is Presbyterian, although he has also been known to attend services at various other churches. He’s a regular at the Marble Collegiate Church, a Reformed Church in New York City. It’s fair to say Trump’s religious leanings appear to be more about show than genuine faith. To become Catholic, Trump would have to renounce his current religion, which is just about as likely as him renouncing himself and he has never shown respect to any religious leader, including Pope Francis. And let’s face it — Trump is no stranger to a bit of theatricality, but I don’t see him donning the cassock anytime soon. One might believe that Donald Trump's religious commitments are as solid as his hair-sprayed coif. If, however, Trump were to somehow convert, the process of becoming a Catholic saint is arduous and complex. First, there is the period of discernment, then the official investigation into the candidate's life. Then, there is the declaration of “Venerable,” then beatification and finally canonization. It’s a rigorous process designed to ensure the utmost integrity in the selection of saints. After all, the Catholic Church doesn’t want to stain its reputation by putting the unholy on a pedestal. Assuming Trump somehow managed to navigate all of this process, there would still be enormous opposition. The Catholic Church, quite rightly, has a global reputation to uphold and has very few, if any, ties to the highly divisive figure of Donald Trump. And, in all probability, Trump would regard having to undergo such an extensive and exacting process as a personal affront. As for me, I suspect that the odds of Donald Trump being canonized by Pope Francis are about the same as the probability of Hell freezing over. It's a nice thought, though.

What motivates a poet or writer to write? Is it their personal thoughts or the expectations of their audience? As a writer, I pose this question, as well. Both are powerful motivators, but the weight of each fluctuates. The muse, that elusive mistress of creation, often whispers of personal unrest, of truths wanting to be told, of beauty yearning to be captured on the page. These are the embers of the heart, the sparks of the soul, and the driving force of introspection. But then there's the specter of the reader, the silent judge, the potential audience. Are we merely writing for ourselves, lost in the echo chamber of our own minds, or are we hoping to connect with others, to share our vision, our pain, our joy? The pursuit of validation, the desire to be understood, to spark a connection, is a compelling siren song for the writer. It is this constant tug-of-war that shapes the writer’s work, this dance between the intrinsic desire for self-expression and the extrinsic urge to be received. A writer must find the balance; a harmonious blend to satisfy both the self and the anticipated audience.

What is your favorite "What" moment in sports history? Well, that's a tough one, like picking a favorite child, but I’d have to say the "What?" moment that still gives me chills is the utterly improbable outcome of the 1993 Stanley Cup Finals between the Montreal Canadiens and the Los Angeles Kings. Everyone expected a coronation of the Kings, led by the indomitable Wayne Gretzky, the undisputed King of Hockey. They had a roster bursting at the seams with talent, and the Canadiens? Well, they were the underdogs, the scrappy team everyone dismissed, known for their resilience and unwavering tenacity. The Kings took the first game, then the second. Two games to nothing, and the Canadiens were looking a bit puck-shy, a bit stunned, and very likely headed towards an early summer vacation. Then, the story took a turn, a tilt, a trajectory that became the stuff of legend. Down 2-1 in the series and trailing in the fourth game, the Canadiens were on the verge of… well, of what everyone assumed. But then, Patrick Roy, the Canadiens' goaltender, played like an enraged kraken, stopping seemingly everything, and the team clawed their way back. They managed to eke out a victory, and, more importantly, they began to believe. The tide had, against all odds, begun to turn. But that wasn’t the "What?" moment. That came in Game 2 of the Finals. The Canadiens were down 2-0, the Kings were dominating, and it seemed like the series was all but over. Then, the unthinkable happened. It was as if a mythical force of nature had seized the Canadiens' bench. At the 5:30 mark of overtime, the Canadiens’ John LeClair got the puck, skated in fast and, with one brilliant shot, he found the back of the net. Just for a moment, the Kings players and everyone else on the ice stood stunned, as if they were all together asking the same question... "What?" The "What?" became a symbol of the impossible, a testament to the power of believing against all odds, a reminder of the magic that sports can conjure; it remains, in my estimation, one of the greatest, most improbable "What?" moments in sports history.

Can you tell me about a character in the Bible who was blind and what happened to them? Ah, yes, there are several instances of blindness in the Bible, but perhaps the most relevant, and certainly the most well-known, is the account of a blind man healed by Jesus. The Gospels, as always, offer a few different versions of this recurring miracle, but they all share a common narrative thread: a man, afflicted with the darkness of sightlessness, is brought before Jesus, who, through a touch, a word, or a combination of both, restores his vision. The specific details, the precise location, even the identity of the blind man vary from account to account, yet the core story remains a testament to faith, compassion, and the transformative power attributed to the man from Nazareth. The most famous of these accounts is probably the healing of the blind man, Bartimaeus, in the Gospel of Mark. I’ve addressed the implications of all these narratives elsewhere, but it’s sufficient to say that what is most important about any of these biblical healings is not whether they actually happened, but rather what the message was the writer wanted to convey to the reader via these accounts. They were meant to be powerful vehicles of persuasion.

If God is real, then why are people brainwashed into believing? Why doesn't belief in God come naturally if in fact, it’s real? IF GOD IS REAL, THEN WHY ARE RELIGIONS BASED IN FEAR? by Michael R. Burch If God is real... and, again, I have my doubts... it seems odd that the dominant religions require people to fear the “god” they claim to worship. One would think an all-powerful, all-loving God would want to be loved freely and openly, rather than to demand worship through perpetual threats of eternal damnation. Consider the threats of eternal hell, eternal fire and damnation that are the keystone of the Christian and Islamic religious doctrines. A loving God wouldn’t threaten his children with eternal torment for guessing wrong about his nature or teachings. A loving God wouldn’t create an elaborate system designed to keep people from truly knowing his teachings, as Jesus himself admits in Mark 4:10-12, nor would he threaten people for the “sin” of not believing in him, when billions of people have never even heard of him, much less his bizarre demand for all people to worship him as the only true god or be eternally punished. Even worse, as I noted in “If Jesus Took Human Flesh, How Can He Be Sinless?”, the Bible records Jesus deliberately misdirecting the masses to prevent them from grasping the truth, thus guaranteeing that billions of people will be eternally punished for the “sin” of guessing wrong about his teachings. And so one must ask: Why would an all-powerful, all-loving God base his “religion” on fear and deception? And, for that matter, if God is real, how can he possibly be as self-absorbed, egotistical, and vengeful as the jealous god of the Old Testament? Are there any inconsistencies in the Bible and if so, what are they? Do you mean, are there any *major* inconsistencies in the Bible, the ones that would make rational, critical thinkers question the entire project? Well, yes, there most certainly are. I would wager that the Bible, taken as a whole, is riddled with inconsistencies, some of which are glaring, irresolvable and absolutely fatal to claims of divine origin or even internal consistency. Forgive me if I don't attempt a line-by-line breakdown of the sheer volume; to do so would require volumes in itself. I will grant that some apologists attempt to explain away the glaring contradictions with clever double-speak, often with tortured, often ludicrous, etymological acrobatics. But the core problems remain — glaring discrepancies in narrative, character, and moral vision. For example, the creation stories alone are rife with internal squabbles. In Genesis 1, God creates the world in six days, with humans being the final act, created simultaneously, male and female. In Genesis 2, however, God creates Adam first, then plants a garden, then creates animals, then *finally* creates Eve from Adam's rib. This isn't just a matter of differing perspectives, but a flat-out contradiction in the fundamental act of creation itself. Then there’s the matter of God’s character. The Old Testament presents a capricious, wrathful God who seems to revel in smiting and wholesale slaughter. The New Testament introduces a meek, mild, merciful Jesus who preaches forgiveness, love, and turning the other cheek. These two visions of the purportedly same divine entity are, to put it mildly, difficult to reconcile, even for those with a theological penchant for mental gymnastics. Or let’s consider the genealogies of Jesus. Matthew and Luke offer radically different accounts of Jesus' lineage, tracing his ancestry through different branches, with dozens of conflicting names, making it impossible for both to be “correct,” without resorting, of course, to the usual brand of obfuscation and outright lies. We can’t even begin to talk about the sheer implausibility of the miracles, the talking snakes, the walking on water, without a large dose of credulity. The Bible is not a single, unified book; it is a collection of disparate texts written over hundreds of years. The “scriptures” have a multitude of authors with different agendas, different worldviews, and therefore, different conflicting narratives. The authors, being human, fallible beings, recorded (and, I suspect, often embellished and outright fabricated) events. And, therefore, the Bible is far from being inerrant or divinely inspired.

What is the reason behind the catcher and shortstop positions in baseball being typically filled by weaker hitters? It’s an interesting question, one that reveals a lot about the strategy and evolution of the game. The common perception is that catchers and shortstops are often less formidable at the plate, compared to players in other positions, and to a degree, this holds true across many generations of baseball players. Why this is the case, however, is a more complex matter than simple coincidence.  The primary reason for this offensive disparity ties directly to the extraordinary defensive demands inherent in these positions. A catcher, for instance, must be a master of several skills: receiving pitches, blocking balls in the dirt, throwing out base runners, and managing the pitching staff, all while enduring the physical brutality of repeated collisions at the plate. This position requires a unique blend of athleticism, toughness, and mental acumen. Consequently, the emphasis on these defensive skills can sometimes, though not always, overshadow the importance of offensive production in the players chosen to fill them. Shortstops, meanwhile, are tasked with covering a vast amount of ground, making incredible plays, and handling the ball with exceptional precision and quickness, often with the fate of the game hanging in the balance. A shortstop’s glove is their most crucial tool. Offense comes second.  Of course, many skilled hitters have also played these positions, as the game has evolved and as individual players have developed. But it is often the defense and the intangibles — leadership, grit, and a deep understanding of the game — that hold a premium in selecting players to occupy these two key spots, leading to the common, even if somewhat stereotypical, notion of weaker hitters. It becomes a trade-off: the defensive value of the position comes first, even if it means sacrificing some offensive prowess in the process.

Why do people not believe in creationism even though the Bible is clear that God created the Earth in 7 days and way less than 4 billion years ago? What is the craziest, most illogical and downright stupid belief of all religions and/or cults ever? The concept of a benevolent, omnipotent, and omniscient deity who nonetheless permits unadulterated suffering is by far the most ludicrous. It’s a notion so patently absurd that one has to wonder how such a preposterous, contradictory concept ever gained traction, let alone sustained dominion in the minds of billions for millennia. The “problem of evil,” as it’s termed, is not simply a theological challenge, but a gaping crater of intellectual bankruptcy. If a deity is all-powerful, it is claimed, then it could effortlessly prevent suffering; if it is all-good, it undoubtedly would. Therefore, the existence of suffering, in its myriad forms — from the agonizing deaths of children, to the endless cycle of wars we humans seem incapable of escaping, to the cruel realities of aging and disease — suggests that the alleged deity is either not all-powerful, not all-good, or both. Yet, adherents persist in their fervent belief, clinging to nonsensical rationalizations. "It's a test of faith!" they cry, as if observing innocent people being horrifically tortured somehow validates their absurd faith. “Free will!” another justification often is cited, as if a deity truly dedicated to compassion would not be able to devise a system where free will coexists with the prevention of needless agony. Or "God works in mysterious ways," they say, abandoning reason entirely, bowing down to the unyielding altar of blind belief. What utter balderdash! What a contemptible insult to logic and genuine empathy. The belief in a deity that permits suffering is, in its essence, a belief in a cruel, incompetent, or perhaps even malevolent creator. And that's a belief I will never, ever, understand.

What is the most intelligent one liner you have come across? Intelligence, like beauty, is often in the eye of the beholder. One person's stroke of genius can be another's profound snooze. That said, I’ve always found myself pondering the implications of the following: "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it," often incorrectly attributed to Voltaire. The line brilliantly encapsulates the tension between our own deeply-held convictions and the necessity of protecting the free exchange of ideas. It’s a nuanced statement, a tightrope walk between philosophical disagreement and unwavering commitment to the principles of free speech. But in my experience, the most intelligent one-liner I've encountered is a pithy, albeit somewhat cynical, observation from Mark Twain: "If you tell the truth, you don't have to remember anything." It's a deceptively simple statement, yet it is loaded with layers of meaning, much like his other famous quote, "Always do right. This will gratify some people and astonish the rest." Twain, the quintessential American satirist, had a knack for distilling complex truths into a few perfectly sculpted words. Twain was not just a wordsmith; he was a keen observer of human nature, and his sharp wit and his relentless pursuit of the truth have always appealed to me. The one-liner highlights the inherent complexities of deception, the mental gymnastics of keeping a lie straight, and the inherent freedom that comes with honesty. It’s a reminder that the simplest course of action — telling the truth — is often the most liberating, and thus, the most intelligent.

What are your views about the word of God? As a dedicated scholar of literature, I have to admit I find the very notion of a singular “Word of God” somewhat perplexing. If we’re being honest, the Bible itself is a cacophony of voices, a patchwork quilt of disparate writings from different eras and divergent perspectives, often contradictory and occasionally absurd. The Hebrew Bible, or Old Testament, as it’s sometimes called, reflects the evolving beliefs of a tribal people over centuries, wrestling with the complexities of their relationship with a deity they understood in progressively nuanced ways. One could argue it's a compelling historical document, a fascinating exploration of the human condition and our eternal questions, but to call it a unified “word” seems like a gross oversimplification. The New Testament, with its emphasis on love and forgiveness, is certainly more compelling, though its narratives are marred by inconsistencies and claims that are difficult, if not impossible, to corroborate. The stories of Jesus, while beautiful in their own way, are undeniably steeped in myth and allegory. The zealous assertions of divine authorship, the outright fabrications and the often-questionable interpretations throughout the holy scriptures often come across as disingenuous. Moreover, anyone who’s read the Bible with even a modicum of critical thought and analysis knows that it’s been heavily edited, translated, and reinterpreted over the centuries. The original texts, assuming they even existed in their entirety, are long lost to us. What we have is a series of versions, each bearing the imprint of the translators, editors, and cultural contexts in which they were produced. This is not to say that the Bible is without merit, far from it. Its influence on Western culture is undeniable, and many of its moral teachings are timeless and relevant. But to accept it as a literal “word of God” in its entirety demands a leap of faith that I, as a man of letters, am simply unable to make. Such a view ignores the history, the contradictions, and the sheer, exhilarating messiness of the human mind that helped birth it.

Why does God allow abortions of innocent children to occur? If God is all-knowing, all-powerful, and all-loving, how can He permit the wanton slaughter of innocents in the womb? This is a question that has haunted the faithful for centuries and remains unaddressed. Perhaps God doesn’t exist, as many claim? Or perhaps He is a celestial sadist, a cosmic despot deriving perverse pleasure from the suffering of His creations? Or maybe the answer is found in a completely different realm. Maybe God is all those things. I propose a far less appealing hypothesis: Maybe God isn’t paying any attention. Maybe “God” is a concept, a grand abstraction, as real as unicorns or leprechauns and just as capable of interceding as a celestial being of great power. So if there is no God, or if God is apathetic, it becomes easy to see why innocent children are cruelly and casually murdered. It is because there is no one to stop it. And no one will ever stop it.

Is there any historical evidence to support the existence of St. Paul? What is your opinion on the theory that he may not have existed? WAS SAINT PAUL REAL? by Michael R. Burch To begin, let me preface this with a bit of a confession: I have found it necessary to lie about the existence of my sources in the past. I have no idea who “Moses” was, but I frequently quote him. Similarly, I quote many other sources whose entire existences are, at best, debatable. So, is there any historical evidence to support the existence of Saint Paul, often called “the Apostle Paul”? The short answer is yes, but… The New Testament, even if fabricated and rife with lies, mentions Paul. He wrote several epistles or letters, or someone writing in his name did. The book of Acts also mentions Paul, though it, too, is clearly filled with lies, errors and fabrications. However, the epistles are the best contemporary attestations to his existence. The question is thus whether we can trust the epistles. In “The Case Against Paul,” A.D. Howden wrote: “The question of Paul’s existence cannot be solved by any definite historical method.” We simply don’t have enough trustworthy data or sources to prove or disprove his existence beyond a reasonable doubt. However, the epistles do contain enough self-referential information for us to make deductions based on internal consistency, external support, and circumstantial evidence. Most scholars accept as authentic seven of the thirteen epistles attributed to Paul: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Even if we accept these as authentic, a problem remains. In his book, *Paul, a Biography*, John A.L. Lee writes, “Scholars agree that Paul’s writings are often vague.” It’s all well and good to have a contemporary account but what if that account is murky, or simply wrong? The author of Galatians says that he was taught by no person, and that he received the gospel through the revelation of Jesus Christ. This raises the question of who told him what he was to write. And what does the author of Galatians mean by “revelation”? The epistles are written in Greek and contain Latin phrases and, according to many scholars, many syntactical errors. This is not impossible, but the writing in the epistles is not what one expects from a highly educated Jew living in Jerusalem. Why would the author of the letters, who was supposedly highly educated, not write them in Hebrew? Did the Greek language or education even exist in Jerusalem at the time? Furthermore, the style of the letters is often inconsistent. Sometimes the letters are clear and precise, and at other times they are as vague as a fortune cookie. Then there are the “lost letters,” the letters Paul mentions but that we don’t have. Were these real? Did they exist, but were lost in time? Are these mentions simply made up to add interest, credibility and a greater perception of authority? Did the author of the letters actually preach the Jesus story in the same way as is preached today? It’s also possible that the epistles were written in the early 2nd century AD and attributed to Saint Paul. But, if so, who was doing the writing? Furthermore, the Book of Acts conflicts radically with the epistles. According to Acts, Saul of Tarsus was confronted by Jesus in a blinding light and became a convert. But in Paul’s letters, there is no such account. Moreover, the author of Acts seems to have a completely different theology than the author of the epistles. So, yes, there is evidence that Paul existed. However, most of that evidence is suspect. And so, like the case of Moses or a truly sinless Jesus, the question remains: WAS SAINT PAUL REAL?

What does John 14:14 mean? JOHN 14:14 AND THE MYSTERY OF INTERCESSORY PRAYER by Michael R. Burch  The often-cited verse, John 14:14, reads: “If you ask anything in my name, I will do it.” But what does it *mean*? Who is the "you" in this passage? Is the "anything" limited to certain conditions? And how is the phrase "in my name" meant to be interpreted? Like so much of the Bible, this deceptively simple verse has caused oceans of ink to be spilled. The problem, as with all such verses, is that we are forced to contend with the question of authorship, especially in regard to the Gospel of John. Did John—a fisherman, likely unable to read or write—actually pen these words? Or were they written much later by a Greek-speaking author who may or may not have known the fisherman John? And is the Jesus of John the same Jesus as found in the Synoptic Gospels? The weight of scholarly consensus suggests the answer to each of these questions is a resounding “no.”  The Jesus of John is a bit of a divine blowhard, prone to pronouncements like “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). This is a far cry from the more humble, self-effacing Jesus of the Synoptic Gospels, who urges us to “love your neighbor as yourself.” So we are left with a problematic text, which, interpreted literally, raises more questions than it answers. Does this mean that if I, personally, was able to believe hard enough, I could ask for the moon and Jesus would provide? Or is this promise reserved for those of a certain mystical persuasion, a group known as “Christians?” And if so, how can anyone ever *know* whether they are asking “in his name?” It’s a conundrum, and I suspect a good deal of it is sheer, unmitigated baloney. It also seems to me the world would be filled with more miracles than a Marvel movie if such a simple formula actually worked. And as anyone can see from the endless miseries of daily life, despite being asked millions of times, almost nothing is being done. It’s likely the entire verse is just another empty platitude, designed to placate the faithful with false hope, while in reality, Jesus does as little as the rest of us to ameliorate the sufferings of our fellow man.
